## Findings by module

### 3

- **confirmed** (ch-017.txt): Cottenham's arrest in detail (30/03/1908, Columbiana depot; deputy Newton Eddings): charged with riding a freight without a ticket; judge convicted both Cottenham and Monroe Dolphus of vagrancy though no evidence was offered; sentence three months' hard labour for Tennessee Coal, Iron & Railroad, with fees of $38.40 (Cottenham) and $31.85 (Dolphus) added: Cottenham +3 months 6 days, Dolphus +2 months 20 days; TCI paid the county $12 a month per man; deputy delivered 60+ men in 12 months and was paid per prisoner; sheriff's fee system (Fine and Forfeiture Fund) gave officials a profit motive; Slope No. 12 stockade, chained barracks of ~200 men, bloodhounds, nightly whippings. Arithmetic check: a 30-day sentence in the introduction extended to 'nearly a year' conflicts with this chapter's 'three months of hard labour' plus fees (3 months + 3 months 6 days = about 6 months): Blackmon's introduction (30 days, nearly a year) and chapter XIII (3 months + 3 months 6 days) do not match; treat the duration as unsettled and avoid quoting a single figure [internal inconsistency in the book]. Governor Cole Blease's quoted pardons show official attitudes. Fee-based policing as incentive structure is analogous to the Congo agent commission system in Hochschild (incentives drive coercion) -- a useful cross-module comparison
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Blackmon's thesis and evidence base (use as the documented counter-example to the Willie Lynch hoax, Module 3 lesson 4): convict leasing and peonage in the post-Reconstruction US South as a forced-labour system 'slavery by another name', documented from county court records, Department of Justice files (30,000+ pages of debt-slavery cases at the National Archives), company papers and letters (e.g. Carrie Kinsey to President Roosevelt, 31/07/1903, file 12007). Case: Green Cottenham, 22, arrested 30/03/1908 in Shelby County, Alabama for 'vagrancy', sentenced to 30 days' hard labour extended to almost a year by fees, leased to Tennessee Coal, Iron & Railroad (a US Steel subsidiary) for a payment of $12 a month to the county, task 8 tons of coal a day; ~60 men died at Slope 12 that year. Scale: Blackmon's own estimate 'more than a hundred thousand and perhaps more than twice that' caught in the system [ESTIMATE, his inference]. Key claim: 1901 complete disenfranchisement coincided with the system; it largely ended around WWII (peonage prosecutions 1940s). He stresses it differed from antebellum slavery (not lifelong, not hereditary), i.e. the 'slavery' label is his argument; historians such as Oshinsky ('worse than slavery') and Lichtenstein emphasise convict leasing specifically. For Module 3: shows the African-American context in which Garvey, Du Bois and Pan-Africanism arose, with documents available to verify claims, unlike the fabricated letter. Findings limited: Blackmon does not discuss Africa, Garvey, Pan-Africanism or the Willie Lynch letter
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Background chapter on the aftermath of emancipation in Bibb County, Alabama (1865-68): Freedmen's Bureau; the '40 acres' promise (Sherman's field order for 400,000 acres in South Carolina early 1865, rescinded by Andrew Johnson; rumours persisted to 1868); Greene County whites burned the courthouse and 1,800 wage suits in 1868; coercive 1865-66 labour contracts that 'echoed slave laws' (pass requirements, no firearms) mostly dissolved by Union commanders; industrial slave-leasing before the war (Bibb Steam Mill, Brierfield Iron Works, Confederate impressment of slaves). Shows continuity from slave hiring to convict leasing -- the kind of documented continuity absent from the Willie Lynch text. A passing detail: the African-born ancestor Scipio (born c.1802) illustrates the late Atlantic slave trade into the US South. No direct bearing on African modules beyond diaspora context
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Documented origin of convict leasing (the real forced-labour system the Willie Lynch hoax lesson can be contrasted with): Thirteenth Amendment (1865) allows involuntary servitude as punishment for those 'duly convicted'; post-war Black Codes: vagrancy laws (all former Confederate states but Arkansas and Tennessee by end of 1865), Mississippi 1865 annual labour-contract law, discharge-paper laws, 1880s laws in Alabama, North Carolina and Florida criminalising a Black worker changing employers; Alabama leased its 374 state prisoners for $5 in 1866 (a sham front for a railroad whose president the governor later became); Texas 1866 (250 convicts at $12.50/month), Georgia 05/1868 (100 convicts for $2,500), Mississippi 1868 (241 prisoners to Richardson, then to Nathan Bedford Forrest in 1871, a KKK co-founder 1866), Tennessee 1871 (nearly 800 to a founder of TCI), North Carolina 1872, South Carolina 1877; by 1877 every ex-Confederate state except Virginia leased convicts; Alabama convict mortality ~20 per cent in first two years, 35 per cent in the third, nearly 45 per cent in the fourth (Blackmon's reading of state records). Antebellum precedents: railroads owned ~20,000 slaves by 1861; Milner's 1859 argument that Black industrial labour under a white overseer would be profitable. All figures are Blackmon's reading of archives; a US-focused history, to be cited in Module 3 only for context. Also confirms: the claim that the South's laws targeted Black people was rarely explicit in text but 'widely understood' in enforcement
- **extended** (ch-021.txt): End of the system (documented, with figures): Georgia 1930 -- over 8,000 men, nearly all Black, in chain gangs in 116 counties despite 'abolition' of convict leasing in 1908; Alabama 1927: 37,701 misdemeanour arrests subject to sale by sheriffs, one in nineteen Black men over twelve in some form of involuntary servitude (Blackmon's calculation); Alabama 1928 arrest categories (12,500+ alcohol, 2,735 vagrancy, 2,014 gaming, 458 leaving an employer's farm, 154 adultery). Two Mississippi sheriffs earned $20,000-$30,000 each in 1929 from selling labour; Macon 1932 sixty vagrancy arrests delivered to a planter. Federal turn: Attorney General Francis Biddle's Circular No. 3591 on 12/12/1941 (five days after Pearl Harbor) ordering prosecution of peonage as 'involuntary servitude and slavery'; first modern slavery prosecutions (U.S. Sugar in Florida; Skrobarcek case, Beeville, Texas, 1942); statutes sharpened 1948 and 1951. The motive was wartime propaganda (Axis broadcasts on US racism). Reading: the system ended with WWII federal pressure -- a point of contrast with the Willie Lynch letter's alleged 'lasting 300 years'. Used as context for Module 3 only. Slight arithmetic note: 'One in nineteen' = 5.3 per cent of Black males over 12 in Alabama (1927)
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Blackmon's UK preface (2012): says the system extended American slavery by 'almost 80 years' and compares in tone to the persecution of European Jews (an author's analogy, not a finding); Pulitzer Prize (general non-fiction) 2009; his scope is the US South 1865-1945. For this course the book is only diaspora context (convict leasing and peonage) and a contrast case to the Willie Lynch hoax: Blackmon documents a real forced-labour system from court and company records, whereas the 'Willie Lynch letter' has no documentary source. Findings from this book are therefore limited
- **note** (epilogue ch-022 end): Blackmon's epilogue ends at the unmarked Pratt City mine-camp burial site of Green Cottenham: no surviving grave marker. Memorial detail only; no new fact for Module 3. Scope stays limited to US convict leasing context.

Totals: 1 confirmed, 0 refined, 0 contradicted, 4 extended, 0 absent, 2 note.
